title: Contracts Review: Safe by Design
story: You've learned all three contract tools: `requires:` guards inputs, `ensures:` verifies outputs, and `invariant:` maintains data integrity forever. Now it's time to practice them all together — on math functions, string operations, structs with methods, and real-world validation. Contracts aren't comments — they're machine-checked guarantees. And you can now write them fluently.
why: This review synthesizes requires, ensures, and invariants into a unified mental model — after this lesson, you'll instinctively add contracts to every function and type you write.
analogy: Writing contracts on every function and type is like installing smoke detectors in every room of your house. One detector is better than none, but a fire in the kitchen doesn't help if the detector is in the bedroom. Contracts everywhere — requires on every function that takes parameters, ensures on every function that returns values, invariants on every struct with rules — means bugs can't hide. The smoke detector goes off the moment smoke appears, no matter which room it's in.
try_it: Write `safe_substring(s: Str, start: Int, length: Int) -> Str` with three requires and one ensures. Test it with valid indices. Test it with start=-1 (should trap). Test it with start+length too large (should trap). Write `safe_sqrt(x: Float64) -> Float64` with both requires and ensures. Write a `Counter` type with `invariant: count >= 0;` and methods `increment`, `decrement` (must clamp to 0), and `reset`. Does every method maintain the invariant?
tips: Make contracts a habit: every new function gets a requires if it has constraints on inputs
ensures is most valuable on functions where the body is non-trivial — it catches logic errors, not just input errors
Invariants on types save you from writing the same requires on every method — declare it once on the type
Contracts are checked in both debug AND release builds — they're not just development tools
common_mistakes: Over-contracting — not every function needs contracts; simple getters and setters may not need them
Writing contracts that are too expensive to check — `ensures: result == sorted_copy_of_input;` would re-sort on every call
Forgetting that contracts don't replace tests — they complement tests by catching different kinds of bugs
